meta.title: Check your understanding: The band gap

objectives: Explain why any single band gap wastes part of sunlight, both below and above the gap
Calculate the longest wavelength a material can absorb from its band gap
Describe what the Shockley–Queisser limit is and how stacking gaps gets past it

questions.prompt: Germanium's band gap (0.66 eV) lets almost every photon in sunlight be absorbed. Why is its single-junction limit still well below silicon's?
choices: It lets too many photons pass straight through unabsorbed
Most of each absorbed photon's energy is lost as heat above the low gap
Its gap is direct, so it needs a much thicker absorber
Germanium reflects most of the sunlight that reaches it
questions.explain: A low step lets nearly every photon in, but each one keeps only 0.66 eV and loses the rest as heat; set the widget to 0.66 eV and more than half of the Sun's power lands in the heat slice. Photons passing straight through is the problem of a high gap, the opposite case.

questions.prompt: The perovskite methylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI₃) has a band gap of about 1.61 eV. Using λ_g = hc ÷ E_g with hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm, what is the longest wavelength it can absorb?
questions.explain: 1240 ÷ 1.61 ≈ 770 nm, at the red edge of visible light, so this perovskite misses the near-infrared that silicon (cutoff 1107 nm) still catches. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 1997 nm; a wider gap always means a shorter cutoff wavelength.

questions.prompt: This page's chart peaks at about 30.5 %, yet the Shockley–Queisser limit is usually quoted as about 33 %. Why the difference?
choices: The chart includes real-cell losses such as reflection and resistance
The 33 % is for a stack of two cells, not a single one
The chart is for silicon only, and 33 % is for gallium arsenide
They use different light: a blackbody sun above the atmosphere, or the sea-level AM1.5G spectrum
questions.explain: Both are ideal single-junction limits; only the sunlight differs. The blackbody sun above the atmosphere includes ultraviolet and far-infrared power no single gap uses well, while the standard sea-level spectrum (AM1.5G) has much of that stripped out, so more of what is left is usable. Neither number includes real-cell losses.

questions.prompt: To beat the single-gap limit, a tandem stacks two cells with different band gaps. How should they be arranged?
choices: Wide gap on top to take the high-energy photons, narrow gap underneath for the rest
Narrow gap on top, so that it absorbs the most photons first
Two cells with the same gap, so that the voltage doubles
Either way round, as long as the two gaps add up to about 1.34 eV
questions.explain: Each colour should meet a gap that wastes little of it. A wide-gap top cell takes the blue end and lets lower-energy light through to the narrow-gap cell below. With the narrow gap on top it would absorb almost everything and lose the surplus as heat, leaving the wide-gap cell nothing it can use.
